overview.headline: PCR amplifies small DNA segments for laboratory analysis

keyPoints.point: Students learn that PCR is a fast and inexpensive technique used to amplify small segments of DNA
keyPoints.quote: the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a fast and inexpensive technique used to "amplify" - copy - small segments of DNA.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that repeated cycles of denaturing and synthesizing can produce more than one billion exact copies of DNA
keyPoints.quote: leading to more than one billion exact copies of the original DNA segment.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that Taq polymerase builds new strands of DNA using original strands as templates
keyPoints.quote: Next, an enzyme called "Taq polymerase" synthesizes - builds - two new strands of DNA, using the original strands as templates.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that amplified DNA supports laboratory techniques including DNA fingerprinting and diagnosis of genetic disorders
keyPoints.quote: including DNA fingerprinting, detection of bacteria or viruses (particularly AIDS), and diagnosis of genetic disorders.

keyTerms.gloss: technique that amplifies small segments of DNA for analysis
keyTerms.quote: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a technique used to "amplify" small segments of DNA.

keyTerms.gloss: enzyme that builds new DNA strands using original strands as templates
keyTerms.quote: Next, an enzyme called "Taq polymerase" synthesizes - builds - two new strands of DNA, using the original strands as templates.

keyTerms.gloss: process where heating separates DNA into single stranded pieces
keyTerms.quote: To amplify a segment of DNA using PCR, the sample is first heated so the DNA denatures, or separates into two pieces of single-stranded DNA.

keyTerms.gloss: machine programmed to alter temperature to allow denaturing and synthesis
keyTerms.quote: It is directed by a machine called a thermocycler

keyTerms.gloss: clinical technique for detection and identification using amplified DNA samples
keyTerms.quote: including DNA fingerprinting, detection of bacteria or viruses (particularly AIDS), and diagnosis of genetic disorders.
